record.paper_title: Ductile-to-brittle transition and yielding in soft amorphous materials: perspectives and open questions
record.context_brief: frameworks for shear bands and fluidization time
record.original_question: How many theoretical frameworks are needed to describe the different types of shear bands and the associated timescales in ductile-like and brittle-like materials, and can concepts from nucleation dynamics and dynamical phase transitions predict the fluidization time, the relevant order parameter, and the time-dependent growth of shear-band size?

evidence.quote: A challenging question is to determine how many different theoretical frameworks are needed to describe the various types of shear bands and time scales associated with shear banding.

In all cases, a key quantity to predict theoretically is τ f as a function of the external forcing mechanism and the material properties. The case of transient or long-lived shear bands is particularly interesting because modeling these systems is greatly simplified using a field theoretical approach, i.e., a continuous model, where, however, the choice of the order parameter is crucial. Then, in order to describe quantitatively the time evolution of the system, one needs to predict how the size of the shear band grows in time.

artifact.category_tag: shear banding and yielding in amorphous solids
artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a soft amorphous material (e.g., a yield-stress fluid, gel, emulsion, or glassy solid) subjected to an external mechanical forcing such as an imposed shear stress or shear rate. Upon yielding, such systems can develop heterogeneous flow in the form of shear bands, which may be transient, long-lived, or permanent, and whose phenomenology differs sharply between ductile-like and brittle-like response regimes. Define the fluidization time τ_f as the characteristic time after which the material attains a homogeneous flowing state under the applied forcing, regarded as a function of the forcing parameters and the material properties.

Address the following questions:

(a) Determine the minimal number of distinct theoretical frameworks required to describe the various types of shear bands (transient, long-lived, permanent; ductile-like vs brittle-like) and the associated timescales of their formation and evolution. In particular, decide whether a single unified framework suffices, or whether ductile-like and brittle-like regimes intrinsically demand separate descriptions.

(b) Within a continuum field-theoretical description of yielding, identify an appropriate scalar (or tensorial) order parameter capturing the local fluidization state of the material, and derive predictions for τ_f as a function of the external forcing and material parameters.

(c) Using analogies with classical nucleation theory and dynamical phase transitions, predict the time-dependent growth law for the size ℓ(t) of a shear band from its inception to full fluidization, and characterize the universal exponents or scaling relations governing both ℓ(t) and τ_f across ductile-like and brittle-like regimes.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is posed as an open challenge in the soft matter / yielding literature. Recent reviews on the ductile-to-brittle transition and shear banding in amorphous materials describe the unified theoretical framework, choice of order parameter, and prediction of fluidization time as outstanding open problems, with only partial results from elastoplastic models, mode-coupling-type theories, and nucleation analogies. No comprehensive solution has been reported.

status_evidence.title: Ductile-to-brittle transition and yielding in soft amorphous materials
status_evidence.snippet: Reviews open questions on shear bands, fluidization timescales, and the need for theoretical frameworks combining nucleation and dynamical phase transition concepts.
status_evidence.claim: Identifies the question of how many frameworks are needed and whether nucleation/dynamical phase transition ideas can predict τ_f and shear-band growth as open.

status_evidence.title: Yielding and the ductile-to-brittle transition in amorphous solids (related reviews)
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses elastoplastic and mean-field models of yielding; shear-band dynamics and fluidization remain only partially understood across the ductile-brittle range.
status_evidence.claim: Supports that a unified predictive theory of shear-band growth and fluidization time is not yet established.
